title: The chameleon on the tree
hook: three friends argue about the color of a lizard on a tree, and the man who lives under it settles it
carry: god with form, and beyond every form
tomorrow: what did a young man from that room tell Chicago?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salt doll that went to measure the ocean and never came back to report. Your line: Brahman is known by melting, not measuring.
screen: `THE SALT DOLL AND THE OCEAN.` · `KNOWN BY MELTING, NOT MEASURING.`

segments.voice: Red. I saw it myself, it was red. No, it was green, I was standing right there. You're both wrong, it was blue. Three friends, one tree, one small lizard, and an argument getting louder by the minute. Each of them went into the woods, saw a chameleon on a branch, and came back certain. Ramakrishna told this story to the visitors in his room at Dakshineswar, and the one who settles it isn't any of the three.

In the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, they all walk back to the tree to settle it. A man sitting underneath says: I live here, and I know that creature well. Every one of you is right. Sometimes it's red, sometimes green, sometimes yellow or blue. And sometimes it has no color at all. Ramakrishna gives the meaning plainly. The one who thinks of God constantly comes to know God's real nature, and knows that God shows himself to seekers in many forms and aspects: with qualities, and then again without any. Hindus have names for both. Saguna: God with qualities, the Krishna you can dress, feed and sing to. Nirguna: God beyond every quality and every name. Ramakrishna wouldn't let either side throw out the other. It's the others, he says, who suffer through useless arguments. Notice what the man under the tree does not say. He doesn't tell anyone they made it up. Each friend really did see red, or green. The trouble came with one extra word: only. And his knowledge comes not from a sharper argument but from living there: closeness, not cleverness. His last words, sometimes no color at all, point to where the doll went. That closes a week. It began with Mira's jewel of the name, went out into the lanes of Bengal with Chaitanya's drums, and came to rest at Dakshineswar, where a priest answered questions with a pond, a snake, a doll made of salt, and a lizard on a tree.
screen: `THE MAN UNDER THE TREE.` · `EVERY ONE OF YOU IS RIGHT.` · `SAGUNA AND NIRGUNA.` · `SOMETIMES NO COLOR AT ALL.` · `CLOSENESS, NOT CLEVERNESS.`

segments.voice: Pray today to God in the form you love: a picture or murti of Krishna, Shiva or the Mother, or a name, if that's your way. Then close your eyes and rest a moment in the silence beyond the picture, the part with no color at all. Then bring to mind someone who sees God differently from you, and ask quietly what they saw from where they were standing. If you don't pray, do the last part only.
Ramakrishna. The priest of Dakshineswar, telling of a lizard on a tree that shows every color, and sometimes no color at all.
Your line: God with form, and beyond every form. Tomorrow, one of the young men from that room speaks a long way from home. Day nine hundred thirty-eight, done.

Dakshineswar.meaning: the temple on the Ganges where Ramakrishna lived and taught

Mira.meaning: Mirabai, the princess-poet who sang to Krishna

Chaitanya.meaning: the Bengali saint who took the singing of God's names into the streets

Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna.meaning: the book of his conversations, written down by a visitor called M.
